videos.title: Europe send search and rescue personnel to Venezuela in response to massive quakes
videos.transcript: Europe is deploying rescue teams and other emergency assistance to Venezuela after double earthquakes hit the country on Wednesday leaving at least 920 people dead and more than 50,000 missing according to the UN. So far 520 responders from eight EU member states including [music] Czechia, Spain, Italy, France Luxembourg Germany Portugal and the Netherlands have mobilized for deployment through the EU civil protection mechanism. On Saturday Italian firefighters and 85 [music] French search and rescue personnel were seen arriving to join other international [music] teams in rescue operations. The UK Royal Air Force personnel prepared aid packages to be deployed to Venezuela. Meanwhile, Turkey sent two military aircraft carrying search and rescue personnel, medical teams and humanitarian aid. The two powerful earthquakes struck the northern Yaracuy region within eight minutes of each other on Wednesday night leaving unprecedented damage.
videos.summary: Following two powerful earthquakes that struck Venezuela's northern Yaracuy region on Wednesday, European countries have mobilised search and rescue teams through the EU civil protection mechanism. At least 920 people were killed and more than 50,000 are reported missing according to the UN. Several non-EU countries, including the UK and Turkey, have also sent personnel and humanitarian aid.

videos.title: Macro Matters: Can Europe afford the extreme heat?
videos.transcript: Europe's in a heat wave and the economic thermometer is flashing reds. This is Macro Matters and we're talking about the extreme heat. The ECB has more than inflation to sweat over. A record-breaking heat wave is sweeping across Europe, disrupting businesses and raising fresh questions about the impacts of climate change. Research suggests that these shocks could become harder for policy makers to ignore, hitting growth while pushing up prices at the same time. So, are the economic costs getting too hot to handle? Well, let's ask George Buckley, chief European economist at Namura. So, George, some stress test suggests that by 2030, GDP losses could reach 5 to 7% in the most exposed economies like France and Germany. So, is extreme heat becoming one of the biggest structural threats to Euroone growth? >> I think it probably is, Peter. I mean, the problem is, of course, is that this comes at a time when productivity growth is not particularly high in Europe as it stands. So anything which might dent it even further uh is clearly a risk. Um it's not the job of central banks to directly deal with this but they might have to indirectly deal with it to the extent that if we see for example food prices rising that'll put upward pressure on overall inflation. They might have to do a bit more in terms of tightening policy when maybe no tightening might have been required in order to offset some of that and achieve their inflation goals. And there are a lot of ways that inflation uh might move on account of um on account of climate change. One of course is the impact on on food prices which is probably the most obvious. Uh the other is the impact on maybe some some of the decarbonization strategies that are are being implemented because of course it's costly to do this. Uh it'll push upward pressure on uh prices of of green tech for example. So lot lots of things to think about when it comes to the impact on both productivity and prices. >> As well, Europe's power system is under strain with sharp swings in electricity prices. So after your area inflation moved back above 3% for the first time in over two years, will energy driven price pressures continue to heat up? >> The rise in prices that we've already seen, how much of that will filter through into underlying prices, non-energy prices via indirect effects. So where companies say, "Well, our costs have gone up. we have to pass that on or through second round effects where people say, "Well, I'm now expecting higher inflation. I need to push for higher wages." Now, we haven't seen any of those second round effects as yet, but there are there is certainly evidence to suggest that the indirect effect, the pass through uh into things like transportation costs, into communication prices, they seem to have risen. Whether it's all to do do with the oil increase is questionable, but I I certainly think that notwithstanding the fact that oil prices are now a lot lower than where they were, I still think we're in that situation where we are going to see further increases in inflation before it comes down. >> Let's talk about the fiscal hit, though. For example, extreme heat could cost Germany up to $131 billion by 2030. So, how can the block cope when the heat is turning into a budget pressure cooker? If you think about the way that Europe works, it it's never really been set up, particularly the north of Europe has never been set up to deal with trying to keep um trying to keep the heat out of people's homes and offices. It's always been about trying uh trying to keep the heat in during the winter months. So, this is a a very different situation that we face and we will continue to face as as the globe warms up. uh so you know I imagine we will be losing quite a bit of output over the course of this week as people don't go into work uh kids don't go into school there's been a lot of changes which will have an impact on ours worked uh and therefore output but um you know from the longer term perspective uh this is going to be something which is likely to happen more regularly and and therefore those sort of uh impacts on growth and potentially inflation uh will come through more often. Meanwhile, we did get comments from ECB Schneable this week. She warned that rates may need to go higher to contain price pressures. Do you agree or do you think the ECB is at risk of overheating the economy? >> Even before this crisis, by the way, we were talking about the possible need for the ECB to raise interest rates. The other point is that the ECB now thinks that the neutral uh level of interest rates, the point at which everything is in balance, so where economic growth is running at its trend and inflation's running at target, that point the ECB now thinks is higher than it once was. They think and and certainly Michel thinks it it's higher than than the ECB's um collective view. So I I do think it's it's understandable why she has said what she's said and I wouldn't be surprised and certainly we have in our own forecasts the ECB moving further to tighten policy um on on account of what's been going on in energy markets. >> Finally, George, the EU's US trade deals now set to come into force but Brussels hoping it brings some stability amid global tensions. So does this at least take a bit of heat out of relations with President Trump? >> Will it have a big impact? I mean, the fact that Europe is removing the tariffs that it was setting on industrial goods imports from the US into Europe, I think is encouraging at the margin. I don't think it's the most important thing for inflation, but it will be uh encouraging. The US is also capping um its tariffs at 15%. Um still 15%, but it's less than potentially what it could have been. Um and that also means that it'll be positive for growth. So I think it's a this is one of those things which is actually good for growth and also uh pulls down on inflation and that's what central bankers do like. So I think this is certainly encouraging news. >> That was George Buckley from Namura. Don't forget you can watch more videos on Reuters.com.
videos.summary: This video explores the economic consequences of extreme heat waves in Europe, featuring an interview with George Buckley, chief European economist at Nomura. The discussion covers how rising temperatures affect GDP, inflation, energy prices, and government budgets. The interview also touches on the ECB's response to price pressures and the impact of a new EU-US trade deal.

videos.title: Anthropic claims Alibaba unlawfully copied Claude’s capabilities
videos.transcript: Anthropic has accused Chinese tech giant Alibaba of extracting its claw AI technology in what it says is the largest known attack of its kind. That is according to a letter seen by Reuters. The US AI company said Alibaba carried out a distillation operation earlier this year that involves using outputs from a powerful AI to train a cheaper model, effectively copying its abilities. Anthropic says the operation used nearly 25,000 fake accounts to generate more than 28.8 million interactions with Claude. It linked the campaign to operators affiliated with Alibaba and its AI lab Quinn and it warned that distillation could help China catch up with its advanced capabilities. The accusations remain in a letter sent on June 10th to Senators Tim Scott and Elizabeth Warren ahead of a US Senate Banking Committee hearing on AI back in February. Anthropic said it faced attacks by Chinese AI outfits including Deep Seek. Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest accusations.
videos.summary: Anthropic has accused Chinese tech company Alibaba of secretly copying its Claude AI system through a process called distillation. According to a letter seen by Reuters, Alibaba allegedly used nearly 25,000 fake accounts to generate millions of interactions with Claude in order to train a cheaper AI model. Alibaba has not yet responded to the accusations.

videos.transcript: This is the biggest bi-election I've ever covered. Why? videos.title: 'Absolutely freezing' winter storm causes mass power outages in US. #Storm #Weather #BBCNews
videos.transcript: Well, there are not many people out and about as you can imagine this morning. Most people are hunkering down because this is an absolutely massive storm stretching some 1500 miles across the United States. Here in Washington DC, we're expecting up to a foot of snowfall today. But in other places, southern states for example, people are just having to hang tight. Power has been knocked out. In some states, some people are without ways to heat their homes right now. Other people, they're trying to find some fun where they can. They're out sledging. A few impromptu snowball fights springing up. But certainly, people are just hanging tight because we're expecting some record snowfall. And it's not just the snow. I've got to tell you, it is absolutely freezing here. And that really gets your bonus.
